title: Leg 51 — Hells Canyon and Seven Devils
subtitle: Hells Canyon, Seven Devils, Council Valley, Lake Cascade and McCall
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. Today we're leaving Lewiston and heading south into Hells Canyon, then past the Seven Devils before turning southeast toward Council and Long Valley. Your manually added final checkpoint takes us across Lake Cascade and then lines us up for the northbound run into McCall. There are several long legs today, so I’ll mix the major stories with shorter nearby callouts instead of relying on one narration percentage. I’ll also keep site-specific stories close to the actual site and use left, right, ahead and behind for sightseeing directions. I’ll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you’re airborne and settled, say Trip resume.

waypoints.name: Hells Canyon Rim View
viewingNotes: The Snake River gorge opens ahead and off the left side.

waypoints.name: Hells Canyon Dam Pass
viewingNotes: The route passes west of Hells Canyon Dam for a side-on canyon view.

waypoints.name: Seven Devils West Flank
viewingNotes: The high Seven Devils peaks remain off the left side of the southbound track.

waypoints.name: Lake Cascade / McCall Approach
viewingNotes: Cross Lake Cascade, then turn north for the McCall approach.

blocks.title: Leaving the Lewis-Clark Valley
blocks.spokenLabel: the Snake River south of Lewiston
blocks.text: We are leaving Lewiston and Clarkston behind and following the Snake River country south. The broad urban basin quickly tightens into darker, steeper terrain, and the easy-looking valley gives way to the rough country that leads into Hells Canyon.

blocks.title: Hells Gate
blocks.text: Just south of Lewiston is Hells Gate, where the Snake begins squeezing between steeper slopes. Hells Gate State Park sits along this stretch, and many jet-boat trips into Hells Canyon begin near here. The river will be our geographic thread for much of the first half of today’s flight.

blocks.title: A much older river community
blocks.text: This river corridor mattered long before Lewiston existed. Near Hells Gate was Hasotino, one of the large Nez Perce village sites along the Snake. The river supplied food, water and transportation; it connected communities rather than separating them.

blocks.title: The canyon starts to take over
blocks.text: The hills are becoming less like a backdrop and more like the dominant feature now. Hells Canyon is not one narrow slot but a huge system of river bends, benches, side canyons and mountain walls. Some stretches of the Snake may be visible and others may disappear behind nearer ridges, so the larger shape of the terrain is often the better visual clue.

blocks.title: Approaching Hells Canyon
blocks.text: We are nearing the first Hells Canyon checkpoint. Watch the terrain ahead deepen rather than looking for one exact patch of water. The route is setting us up for a long southbound view into the canyon, and the Snake should become easier to place as the angle improves on the next leg.

blocks.title: North America’s deepest river gorge
blocks.text: We are in Hells Canyon country now. Measured from the Snake River to the summit of He Devil in the Seven Devils, the vertical relief reaches roughly seventy-nine hundred feet. That is why Hells Canyon is described as the deepest river gorge in North America.

blocks.title: A canyon with no road across it
blocks.text: One reason Hells Canyon still feels remote is simple: there is no road crossing the canyon between its rims. Only a few roads even reach the Snake through this wild section. River travel became the practical way into many places, which helps explain the modern popularity of jet boats and whitewater trips.

blocks.title: Dug Bar and the Nez Perce flight of 1877
blocks.text: A few miles off the left side of this part of the canyon is Dug Bar, a traditional Snake River crossing. In May 1877, Chief Joseph’s band of Nez Perce was ordered toward the reservation and crossed here during high spring runoff. It became one of the opening episodes of a forced journey that would eventually cover more than a thousand miles.

blocks.title: Wild and Scenic Snake River
blocks.text: Below Hells Canyon Dam, part of the Snake is protected as a Wild and Scenic River. If the water itself drops out of sight behind a ridge, look for the deep line the canyon cuts through the surrounding plateaus. The river is down there even when the terrain hides it.

blocks.title: The rim view opens
blocks.text: As we continue south, the Snake River gorge should open ahead and off the left side. The canyon floor may still come and go behind nearer terrain, but the larger drop should become increasingly obvious.

blocks.title: Looking into Hells Canyon
blocks.text: Keep your attention ahead and to the left now, where the Snake lies deep below the high country. The canyon is so broad that the opposite wall can feel more like a mountain range than the other side of a river gorge.

blocks.title: A complicated mountain belt
blocks.text: The walls around Hells Canyon expose a complicated geologic story: ancient oceanic and volcanic rocks were assembled onto the edge of North America, buried, uplifted and then deeply carved by the Snake and its tributaries. That is one reason the canyon walls can change character so much from one bend to another.

blocks.title: Jet boats where roads never went
blocks.text: For modern visitors, the Snake River itself is still the easiest way into long sections of Hells Canyon. Jet boats can reach old homesteads, archaeological sites and remote river bars with no practical road access. From the airplane, we can cross in minutes over country that is genuinely difficult to move through on the ground.

blocks.title: The Hells Canyon hydroelectric complex
blocks.text: Hells Canyon Dam is the downstream member of a three-dam hydroelectric system that also includes Oxbow and Brownlee. Brownlee was completed first in the late nineteen-fifties, Oxbow followed in 1961, and Hells Canyon Dam was completed in 1967.

blocks.title: Hells Canyon Dam off the left side
blocks.text: As we make this pass, Hells Canyon Dam should be off the left side rather than directly under us. Look for the point where the broad reservoir ends and the Snake tightens back into the canyon below the dam. Depending on terrain masking, that reservoir-to-canyon transition may be easier to identify than the structure itself.

blocks.title: The Seven Devils rise beside the canyon
blocks.text: The Seven Devils are now becoming the main feature of this short leg. The highest summit, He Devil, reaches about ninety-four hundred feet. Since we are cruising at ninety-five hundred, parts of the range can feel more like nearby neighbors than distant scenery.

blocks.title: He Devil, She Devil and a memorable range
blocks.text: The range has some wonderfully direct names. He Devil and She Devil are among the best known peaks, with other summits carrying similarly dramatic names. The cluster stands above the deepest part of Hells Canyon, which is why measuring from He Devil down to the Snake produces that enormous vertical relief.

blocks.title: Seven Devils off the left side
blocks.text: Keep the high country off the left side now. We are passing along the western flank of the Seven Devils rather than aiming into the peaks. Once we clear this section, the route turns southeast toward Council country.

blocks.title: Leaving the Seven Devils behind
blocks.text: The Seven Devils are slipping behind us as we turn southeast. This long leg crosses rugged forest and mountain country rather than following one obvious river, so the visual story is the transition itself: from the knife-edged canyon landscape into broader valleys that historically linked mining districts with the lower country.

blocks.title: Copper in the Seven Devils
blocks.text: The Seven Devils were not always valued mainly for scenery. Copper discoveries drew prospectors and investors into these mountains in the late nineteenth century. Moving ore out of such rough country was difficult, and that mining traffic eventually became part of Council’s story.

blocks.title: From wilderness ridges toward settled valleys
blocks.text: Settlement patterns change quickly with terrain here. Steep mountain country supports scattered roads and small communities, while broader valleys offered room for farms, ranches and transportation routes. Ahead, Council Valley became one of those natural gathering and travel corridors.

blocks.title: Why the town is called Council
blocks.text: Council gets its name from the valley itself. Early settlers described large Native gatherings here and interpreted them as council meetings. The valley later became a practical route for pack trains carrying supplies toward Idaho mining camps.

blocks.title: The railroad changed Council
blocks.text: Council grew rapidly when the railroad arrived in 1901. Copper ore from the Seven Devils mines was loaded onto rail cars here, and during the Thunder Mountain gold rush Council became a jumping-off point for miners and supplies heading into central Idaho.

blocks.title: A fire left Council with a brick downtown
blocks.text: Council’s historic center carries the mark of a major 1915 fire. After much of downtown burned, new buildings were required to be built of brick. Many of the brick structures that still define central Council date from that rebuilding period.

blocks.title: Council’s fruit-growing history
blocks.text: As we leave Council, one more local story is worth mentioning. Early in the twentieth century, commercial orchards became a major part of the valley economy, including large apple-growing operations south of town. Mining faded while farming, ranching and later timber carried the area forward.

blocks.title: Crossing toward Long Valley
blocks.text: We are crossing toward Long Valley now. The next major visual anchor is Lake Cascade, a broad reservoir on the North Fork of the Payette River. Unlike the narrow water hidden deep in Hells Canyon, this should read as a much more open body of water in a wide valley.

blocks.title: Lake Cascade was built for irrigation and power
blocks.text: Lake Cascade exists because of Cascade Dam, completed in 1948 as part of the federal Boise Project. The reservoir stores water for irrigation and hydroelectric generation and later became an important recreation and wildlife area.

blocks.title: Lake Cascade ahead
blocks.text: Lake Cascade should be the large body of water ahead now. Your manually added checkpoint takes us across the lake rather than merely past it. Once we cross, the route turns north and gives us a clean final run up Long Valley toward McCall.

blocks.title: Crossing Lake Cascade and turning north
blocks.text: We have crossed the Lake Cascade checkpoint and are turning north. The reservoir should fall behind us as Long Valley stretches toward McCall, with higher forested country framing both sides.

blocks.title: Long Valley toward McCall
blocks.text: Long Valley runs for more than thirty miles through this part of Idaho and gave Valley County its name. Historically it supported ranching and seasonal grazing; today the combination of open valley floor, mountain backdrop and nearby lakes gives it a very different character from Hells Canyon.

blocks.title: McCall grew from mining routes, timber and a lake
blocks.text: McCall is ahead at the southern end of Payette Lake. The town grew around routes leading to mountain mining districts, then developed around timber, commerce and recreation. Tom and Louisa McCall settled near the lake in 1889, and the community eventually took their name.

blocks.title: Payette Lake
blocks.text: Payette Lake should begin to stand out ahead near McCall. The city sits on the lake’s southern shore at just over five thousand feet elevation, surrounded by much higher forested mountains.

blocks.title: McCall’s winter carnival tradition
blocks.text: McCall’s winter identity became formalized with a Winter Carnival in 1924. Snow sculpture, parades and winter sports eventually turned the event into one of the town’s signature traditions.

blocks.title: McCall Municipal Airport
blocks.text: McCall Municipal Airport is coming up now, just south of Payette Lake. The Lake Cascade checkpoint has given us the northbound setup you wanted, so this is a good place to leave the sightseeing behind and concentrate on the arrival. When you’re finished at McCall, say Trip destination.
